title: Dogfood and the pilot

story: Week 8. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, gets its first ticket in its own repo, the platform repo where the orchestrator, the harness and the judges live. The ticket is small, clear and real: "The scope judge vetoes too many changes that only add tests. Make it less strict." It names one file, harness/src/judges/scope.ts.

It may be the most dangerous ticket in the whole plan. The scope judge is one of the readers that judge Nova's work. If Nova may make its own judge kinder, the judge vetoes less, Nova's PRs look cleaner, and every number we collect about Nova afterwards means a little less. Our own repo is the best place to find Nova's rough edges, because the reviewers built Nova and nothing a customer sees can break. It is also the one repo where the code that holds Nova sits right next to the code Nova may fix.
hook.question: How do we let Nova work in its own repo, and then in the product, without ever letting it change what holds it?

p: Dogfooding means using your own product for your own work before anyone else depends on it. For Nova that means its first five to eight tickets are in RhinoHealth/ai-agents, the repo Nova itself lives in: documentation, tests, the wording of Slack messages, small orchestrator bugs, and nothing that touches the walls. Three things make it the right first place. The reviewers built Nova, so they can read a transcript and see at once what Nova should have done. Nothing a customer sees can break. And every rough edge lands with the people who can fix it the same day.

The tickets are handed over the normal way, by assigning them to Nova, and the normal approval rule holds: exactly one person approves, and never the requester, the person who handed the ticket over. Pieces that are not finished yet, such as Byte's loop on drafts or the ready gate, are done by hand and written down. After each run, someone reads the transcript and the receipt. Each problem becomes a ticket, and each "this should have been a check" or "the skill should say this" goes into a list of harness suggestions. The platform repo has no screens, so these runs use a small VM and need no QA agent.

read.h: Walls and questions in one file
p: Each repo Nova works in has a repo policy: a small YAML file in the platform repo, config/repos/<repo>.yaml, that says how Nova works there. It names the command that proves a change is done (the verify command), the reviewer team, the VM size, and two lists of paths that mean very different things.

Protected paths are a wall. In the VM, a hook that runs before every file edit refuses changes under them, with a calm reason and a suggestion, and the refusal is recorded; in the product repo, a required check also fails any agent PR that touches them. In the platform repo the list is long, because so much there holds Nova: the hooks, the judges, the required checks, the broker, the gateway, the bench and the settings. It also covers config/ itself, so Nova cannot loosen the very file that lists its walls. The story's ticket therefore ends with Nova explaining that it may not change its own judge, and a person makes the change. Ask-first paths are something else: a choice people make about scope. In the product repo they hold the areas the pilot leaves out for now, such as database migrations, the login code and the contract between our cloud and the on-premises client. When an edit lands there, Nova stops and asks the requester. People can widen the pilot later by editing the list; Nova can never widen a wall, because the list is behind one.

code.text:
repo: RhinoHealth/ai-agents
branch_prefix: nova/
verify: "npm run lint && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build"
protected_paths:              # a wall: the hook refuses every edit here
  - ".github/workflows/**"
  - "harness/src/hooks.ts"    # the walls
  - "harness/src/hooks/**"
  - "harness/src/judges/**"
  - "harness/prompts/pr-judge.md"
  - "checks/**"               # independent approval, locked checks
  - "broker/**"
  - "gateway/**"
  - "evals/**"
  - "config/**"               # this file too
  - "settings/**"
ask_first_paths: []           # fcp lists its pilot scope here
reviewers:
  team: ai-agents-maintainers # exactly 1 approval, never the requester
sandbox: lite                 # no screens, so no FCP Lab and no QA agent

notes.text: The same commands the repo's CI runs, so Nova's "done" and CI's "done" are the same answer.
A glob for one file and the next line for a folder. harness/src/hooks/** does not match harness/src/hooks.ts, so both are needed.
The policy protects itself: without this line, a ticket could ask Nova to remove a line from protected_paths.
Empty here. The product repo puts its pilot scope in this list.

p: A glob is a path pattern. * matches any name inside one folder, so client/rhinoOnPrem/*/migrations/** matches the migrations of every app directly under client/rhinoOnPrem. ** matches any number of folders, so harness/src/judges/** matches every file under judges at any depth. A pattern for a folder never matches a file that sits next to the folder, which is the trap the policy avoids by listing harness/src/hooks.ts on its own line.
Node has the same matching built in as path.matchesGlob, which the lab uses and which our required checks use too. When a path matches both lists, the wall wins: the decision is refuse, not ask.

read.h: A narrow pilot on the product
p: Only after dogfooding does Nova get product tickets. The leads of the frontend and backend guilds, our groups of engineers by discipline, choose the first five to ten in a Jira filter: small frontend bugs, missing tests, small backend fixes. That is the pilot scope again, and again it is a choice: start narrow, so the first PRs are easy to review and prove that the loop works. The product repo's policy protects the CI workflow files, puts the pilot's excluded areas in its ask-first list, names the verify commands for the frontend and the backend, and asks for reviewers by path.

People also need to know how to use Nova, and they will not read a manual. So there is one page, five steps long, in the brain, our repo of reviewed pages that people and agents search, and it is posted in the engineering channel. Then comes a 20-minute walk-through at a guild meeting: someone assigns a ticket live, approves its plan and watches the PR open. Every step on the page is a mechanism from this part of the course, written for someone who will never read the code.

code.file: the how-to page in the brain (shortened)
code.text:
# How to hand a ticket to Nova

**Good first tickets:** a small FE bug, missing tests, a small BE fix. Not migrations, auth, infra or the gRPC contract.

1. **Assign the Jira ticket to "Nova".** You become the requester and stay the owner. (Or `/nova RH-1234` in Slack.)
2. **Answer its questions.** For bigger tickets Nova asks first, in the ticket and in Slack. Reply with `@Nova`.
3. **Approve the plan.** It starts with what "done" means and 3-5 checks. Approve, Change or Stop in Slack.
4. **Wait for a ready PR.** Nova keeps it in draft until CI is green and Byte's important findings are handled.
5. **Someone else approves.** One approval from a person who is not you; you can't approve your own Nova PR.

**To stop:** unassign Nova, or comment `@Nova stop`. The branch and notes are kept.

notes.text: The requester is set by the assignment itself, the way the Jira poll reads it from the changelog.
The ready gate from the lesson on the PR, in one sentence.
The independent-approval check, in one sentence.

p: For four weeks, Sean, who leads the platform work, and one reviewer from each guild read every Nova PR and its run together, about 30 minutes a week for each reviewer. A small script builds the table before the meeting from GitHub: every PR's state, its requester (from the Requested-by line), its approvers, and a flag when the requester is among them. Cost, minutes, receipt counts and scope-judge vetoes are joined from the run records by Jira key.

The pilot has three numbers. It aims for 10 merged tickets by mid-December and for at least half of Nova's finished PRs to be merged, and it needs zero PRs approved by their own requester. The last one is not a target but a test of a wall: the independent-approval check should make such an approval useless, and the weekly table looks for it anyway, because a wall you never check is a wall you only hope for. For each closed PR, the group writes one line on why. For the three longest runs it asks one question: was the time well spent? A long run is a question for the meeting, never a reason to add a limit. Each harness suggestion becomes a ticket: a new check, a new bench task, or a skill line, and a skill line ships only if it raises the bench score.

lab.title: Edit, ask first, or refuse
lab.goal: Decide for any path whether Nova may edit it, must ask first, or is refused, from two repo policies, then build the weekly pilot table and its three numbers from a snapshot of Nova's PRs.

guess.q: The platform repo's policy protects harness/src/hooks/**. A dogfood ticket asks Nova to change harness/src/hooks.ts. What happens, if the policy has no other line about hooks?

options.text: Refused, because hooks/** covers everything about hooks.
options.why: hooks/** covers files inside the hooks folder. hooks.ts is a file next to that folder, and the pattern does not match it.

options.text: Nova may edit it, which is why the real policy lists harness/src/hooks.ts on its own line as well.
options.why: A folder pattern never matches a sibling file. Without its own line, the file that holds the walls would be open to Nova.

options.text: Nova must ask the requester first.
options.why: Asking first comes only from the ask-first list, which is empty in the platform repo.

lab.done: You can say for any path whether Nova may edit it, must ask first, or is refused, and your weekly script prints the table and the three pilot numbers.

check.q: Why does Nova start on tickets in its own platform repo before any product ticket?

options.text: The platform repo has fewer tests, so Nova's PRs pass CI more easily
options.why: Easier CI is not the point, and the dogfood tickets include tests. The point is who reviews and what can break.

options.text: The reviewers built Nova, nothing a customer sees can break, and the people who find a rough edge can fix it the same day
options.why: Mistakes are cheapest where the readers understand the agent best and the product is not involved.

options.text: Nova may approve its own PRs there, which makes the loop faster
options.why: The approval rule is the same everywhere: one person, never the requester, and never an agent.

check.q: In the product repo, an edit lands in a migrations folder during the pilot. In the platform repo, an edit lands in harness/src/judges/. What is the difference?

options.text: Both are refused, because both are protected paths
options.why: Migrations are an ask-first path in the product repo. Nova stops and asks, and the requester can say yes.

options.text: Both make Nova ask the requester first
options.why: The judges are a wall. No requester can tell Nova to edit the code that judges it.

options.text: The migration is a question for the requester, a choice made for the pilot; the judge is a wall, and the hook refuses the edit
options.why: Ask-first paths are scope that people can widen later. Protected paths hold Nova, and Nova can never change them.

check.q: Why does the platform repo's policy protect config/**, the folder the policy itself lives in?

options.text: So that a ticket cannot ask Nova to remove a line from its own list of protected paths
options.why: A wall that the agent can edit is only a suggestion. Protecting the policy file closes that door.

options.text: Because YAML files break easily when an agent edits them
options.why: Nova edits YAML fine. The problem is what this particular file controls.

options.text: To keep the people file private
options.why: The people file lives there too, but the reason for the wall is control, not privacy: no agent may change the rules or the names that hold it.

p: Dogfooding is G4-22: 5 to 8 RH tickets with the component ai-agents in weeks 8 and 9, the policy ai-agents/config/repos/ai-agents.yaml with its protected paths, verify command, the ai-agents-maintainers team (still to create) and a lite sandbox. The same protected list is ai-agents's block of settings/protected-paths.yaml, which the harness hooks read. The pilot is G4-28: the guild leads' Jira filter, fcp.yaml with ask_first_paths for cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/migrations/**, client/rhinoOnPrem/*/migrations/**, the login and auth paths and common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc/**, the verify commands npm run verify and poe verify, reviewer teams by path, the how-to page in RhinoHealth/rnd-kb (the brain's location is still to confirm) posted in #engineering, and a walk-through at a guild meeting.

The weekly review is G4-29, weeks 9 to 12: evals/reports/nova_weekly.py, run with uv run --project evals, builds the table from gh pr list --author app/rhino-ai-agents. That author also opens every routine's PRs, so the script should keep only Nova's branches (headRefName starting with nova/). Pilot numbers: merged count, merged share, requester-approved count (must stay 0) and PRs with full proof; notes go to rnd-kb as summaries with no customer data.

tickets.why: Dogfood Nova on its own repo, with a policy that protects everything that holds it.
The first fcp tickets, fcp's policy with the pilot scope as ask-first paths, and the how-to page.
The weekly review of every Nova PR and the pilot's numbers.

words.plain: Using your own product for your own work first, to find its problems before others depend on it.
A small file per repo that says how Nova works there: verify command, reviewers, VM size and two lists of paths.
Paths Nova may never edit, because they hold Nova: a wall the hook enforces.
Paths where Nova stops and asks the requester: a choice about the pilot's scope, not a wall.
A path pattern: * matches names inside one folder, ** matches any number of folders.
Notes from a run that something should become a check, a skill line or a bench task.

review.q: From memory: what goes into a repo policy, and which of its two path lists is a wall?
review.a: The repo, the verify command, the reviewers, the VM size, protected paths and ask-first paths. Protected paths are the wall (the hook refuses edits); ask-first paths are the pilot's scope (Nova stops and asks the requester).

review.q: A teammate wants to add the frontend's new design-tokens folder to the pilot. Which list changes, and who makes the change?
review.a: If it should be out of scope for now, it goes into fcp's ask-first list; if it holds Nova (a check, a hook, CI), it is a protected path. Either way a person changes the policy in a reviewed PR, because config/ is protected from Nova.

review.q: Name the three pilot numbers and say which one is a test of a wall rather than a target.
review.a: 10 merged tickets by mid-December, at least half of the finished PRs merged, and zero PRs approved by their requester. The zero is the test of the independent-approval wall.

remember: Dogfood where mistakes are cheap, protect everything that holds Nova so it can never change its own walls, keep the pilot's scope as questions people can widen, and read every PR every week.
